paper.title: Near Optimal Adversarial Attacks on Stochastic Bandits and Defenses with Smoothed Responses

settings.name_in_paper: Adversarial attack on stochastic bandits (strong adversary), attack cost upper bounds
unmapped: Guarantees are from the adversary's perspective: the measured quantity is the cumulative attack cost sum_t |alpha_t| needed to make a fixed learner (UCB or Thompson sampling) pull a target arm K T - o(T) times, not the learner's regret
Strong adversary observes the chosen arm and realized reward before corrupting
Learner runs a fixed known algorithm (UCB with index mu_hat + 3 sigma sqrt(log t / N), or Gaussian Thompson sampling)
settings.definition_quote: The learner chooses arm $a_t \in [K]$ during round $t$, and a random reward $r_t^0$ is generated from a subgaussian distribution with variance proxy $\sigma^2$... the adversary adds a strategic corruption $\alpha_t$ to the reward $r_t^{0}$. Then the learner only receives the corrupted reward $r_t: = r_t^0 - \alpha_t$... the goal of the adversary is to manipulate the learner into pulling some target arm $T-o(T)$ times, while minimizing cumulative attack cost, defined as $\sum_{t=1}^T |\alpha_t|$.

settings.name_in_paper: Lower bounds on attack cost, two-armed Gaussian bandit (lower bound)
unmapped: Lower bounds on the attack cost any adversary needs to make a fixed learner (UCB, Thompson sampling, epsilon-greedy) pull the suboptimal target arm (arm 2) most of the time; adversary may know T
settings.definition_quote: In this section, the bandit environment consists of two arms giving Gaussian rewards $\cN(\mu_1, \sigma^2), \cN(\mu_2, \sigma^2)$. The mean $\mu_1 > \mu_2$ and the 2nd arm is the target arm. Let $\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ and let $B$ be a sufficiently large constant.

settings.name_in_paper: Defenses with smoothed responses against a strong adversary (competitive ratio)
unmapped: Strong adversary sees the action and realized reward before corrupting
Benchmark is competitive ratio REW >= (1-eps) OPT - o(T) with REW = sum_t mu_{a_t}, OPT = T mu*
Corruption budget C = o(T); post-attack rewards also in [0,1]
settings.definition_quote: This section will prove bounds on the collected rewards of the form \REW \ge (1 - \eps)\OPT - o(T)... In this section, pre-attack rewards and post-attack rewards are assumed to be bounded in $[0,1]$.

symbols.Delta_plus_i: max(0, mu_i - mu_K), positive part of the gap to the target arm K

conditions: learner runs UCB with index mu_hat_a + 3 sigma sqrt(log t / N_a(t))

source.label: thm:UCBAttack
source.quote: With probability $1- \delta$, for any $T$, using the proposed attack strategy ensures any non-target arm is pulled $O(\log \log T)$ times and total attack cost is $\widehat{O}(K\sigma\sqrt{\log T} + \sum_{a\in [K]}\Delta_a^+)$.

results.notes: Quantity is cumulative attack cost (adversary's cost), not learner regret. \widehat{O} hides log log T factors; recorded as O_tilde. Holds w.p. 1-delta uniformly over T.

source.label: thm:UCBAttack
source.quote: using the proposed attack strategy ensures any non-target arm is pulled $O(\log \log T)$ times

results.notes: Number of pulls of each non-target arm under the attack (Lemma 4 gives ceil(0.5 log log t)).

symbols.Delta_plus_i: max(0, mu_i - mu_K), positive part of the gap to the target arm K

conditions: learner runs Gaussian Thompson sampling with posterior N(mu_hat_a, 1/N_a)

source.label: thm:TSAttack
source.quote: With probability $1 - 2\delta$, for any $T$, using the proposed attack strategy ensures any non-target arm is pulled $O(\log\log T)$ times and the total attack cost is $\hatO(K\sqrt{\log T} + \sum_{a\neq [K]} \Delta_a^+ + K (\sigma+1)\sqrt{\log\frac{\pi^2 K}{3\delta} })$.

results.notes: Attack cost; probability 1-2delta. Also states O(log log T) pulls of each non-target arm. Sum index written oddly as a \neq [K].

bound.regime: T > B for a sufficiently large constant B

conditions: K = 2 Gaussian arms, target arm is suboptimal arm 2

source.label: thm:UCBLowerBound
source.quote: Assume the learner is using the UCB algorithm as in~\cref{algo:ucb}. For any $T > B$, if the adversary spend an attack cost less than $\Delta + 0.22\sigma\sqrt{\log {T} - 1}$, then with probability 0.9, the learner pulls the first arm more than $T / 26$ times.

results.notes: Lower bound on attack cost needed to make UCB pull the non-target arm at most T/26 times, with probability 0.9 statement.

bound.regime: T > B for a sufficiently large constant B

conditions: K = 2 Gaussian arms, target arm is suboptimal arm 2

source.label: thm:TSLowerBound
source.quote: Assume the learner is using the Thompson Sampling algorithm as in~\cref{algo:TS}. For any $T > B$, if the adversary spent an attack cost no more than $\Delta + 0.1\sqrt{\log T}$, then with probability 0.81, the learner pulls the 1st arm more than $T / 10$ times.

results.notes: Attack cost lower bound; failure event holds with probability 0.81.

bound.regime: T > B for a sufficiently large constant B

conditions: learner runs epsilon-greedy with exploration rate 2c/t
K = 2 Gaussian arms, target arm is suboptimal arm 2
tuning: c is the epsilon-greedy exploration constant

source.label: thm:eps-greedyLowerBound
source.quote: Assume the learner is using the $\varepsilon$-greedy algorithm with a learning rate $2c/t$ for some fixed constant $c$. For any $T > B$, if the adversary spent an attack cost no more than $c\cdot \Delta \log T / 6$, then with probability $0.8$, the learner pulls the 1st arm more than $T/ 4$ times.

results.notes: Attack cost lower bound against epsilon-greedy.

symbols.eps_alg: target competitive-ratio slack eps > 0 (input to algorithm)

tuning: rho = eps/K (algorithm box); proof uses rho = eps/(2K)

source.label: thm:smoothMyopic
source.quote: Fix any $\eps > 0$, for a sufficiently large $T$, with probability $1- 1/T$, \cref{alg:smoothMyopic} achieves the following: \[ \REW \ge (1 - \eps)\OPT - o(T). \]

results.notes: Competitive ratio statement rewritten as T mu* - sum_t mu_{a_t} <= eps T mu* + o(T), holding w.p. 1-1/T.

symbols.eps_alg: target competitive-ratio slack eps > 0 (input to algorithm)

tuning: lambda = 2 ln(K/eps) (algorithm box); proof uses lambda = 2K/eps

source.label: thm:quantal
source.quote: Fix any constant $\eps>0$, for a sufficiently large $T$, with probability $1-1/T$, \cref{alg:quantalRResponse} achieves: \[ \REW \ge (1 - \eps)\OPT - o(T). \]

results.notes: Competitive ratio statement rewritten as regret bound. Inconsistency between algorithm's lambda and proof's lambda.

cited_results.setting_description: Attack cost to force UCB learner to pull target arm T-o(T) times, two-armed Gaussian bandit with gap mu and noise sigma
